arXiv:1401.1937v1 [cond-mat.supr-con] 09 Jan 2014

Quasiparticle generation efficiency in superconducting thin-films

T. Guruswamy, D. J. Goldie and S. Withington Affiliation: Detector and Optical Physics Group, Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge, J J Thomson Avenue, Cambridge, CB3 0HE, UK Email: d.j.goldie@mrao.cam.ac.uk
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Thin-film superconductors with thickness ∼30−500​nm~\sim 30-500\,\,{\rm nm} are used as non-equilibrium quantum detectors for photons, phonons or more exotic particles. One of the most basic questions in determining their limiting sensitivity is the efficiency with which the quanta of interest couple to the detected quasiparticles. As low temperature superconducting resonators, thin-films are attractive candidates for producing quantum-sensitive arrayable sensors and the readout uses an additional microwave probe. We have calculated the quasiparticle generation efficiency ηs\eta_{s} for low energy photons in a representative, clean thin-film superconductor (Al) operating well-below its superconducting transition temperature as a function of film thickness, within the framework of the coupled kinetic equations described by Chang and Scalapino.[J. J. Chang and D. J. Scalapino, J. Low Temp. Phys. 31, 1 (1978)]. We have also included the effect of a lower frequency probe. We show that phonon loss from the thin-film reduces ηs\eta_{s} by as much as 40%40\% compared to earlier models that considered relatively thick films or infinite volumes. We also show that the presence of the probe and signal enhances the generation efficiency slightly. We conclude that the ultimate limiting noise equivalent power of this class of detector is determined by the thin-film geometry.

I Introduction

Superconductive detectors have revolutionized experimental astrophysics. Many of these detectors exploit Cooper pair-breaking in a thin-film low transition temperature superconductor operating at low reduced temperatures T/Tc≃0.1T/T_{c}\simeq 0.1 (TT is the temperature and TcT_{c} is the superconducting transition temperature, Tc∼1​KT_{c}\sim 1\,\,{\rm K}). These detectors rely on non-equilibrium effects but to our knowledge no detailed microscopic description exists of the efficiency with which the excess quasiparticles are created in a thin-film superconductor of thickness ∼30−500​nm~\sim 30-500\,\,{\rm nm}. This problem is very relevant not just for kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs),[1, 2] but also for superconducting tunnel junction detectors,[3] single photon counting nanowires,[4] and quantum capacitance detectors.[5] All of these devices can be fabricated by photolithography usually on a relatively thick substrate such as Si or sapphire that is held at TT and that functions as a heat bath. KIDs are thin-film superconducting resonators that can be configured as ultra-sensitive detectors of signal photons across the electromagnetic spectrum. KIDs are typically readout with a microwave probe with photons of energy h​νp∼0.05​Δh\nu_{p}\sim 0.05\Delta, where νp\nu_{p} is the probe frequency, 2​Δ2\Delta is the low temperature superconducting energy gap and hh is Planck’s constant. In this instance understanding combined effects of the signal and the probe is clearly important. In Ref. 6 we described a detailed microscopic calculation of the spectrum of the non-equilibrium quasiparticles and phonons in a superconducting resonator operating at T/Tc=0.1T/T_{c}=0.1 considering only a probe. Ref. 7 compared that model with precise experimental measurements of the temperature and power dependence of the behavior of ultra-sensitive Al resonators, finding good agreement between model and measurement.

In a superconductor each absorbed signal photon with energy h​νs≥2​Δh\nu_{s}\geq 2\Delta breaks a pair (νs\nu_{s} is the signal frequency). Probably the most important consideration in calculating the detection sensitivity of these photons in any thin-film superconducting detector is ηs\eta_{s} the average fraction of the photon energy that creates low energy quasiparticles E∼ΔE\sim\Delta where EE is the quasiparticle energy. We distinguish the primary spectrum of quasiparticles generated by the signal from the driven quasistatic population that is established as the primary spectrum relaxes temporally and energetically. Absorbed photons create a spectrum of excess primary quasiparticles that relaxes to energies E∼ΔE\sim\Delta by emitting phonons on a timescale τcascade∼0.1​–​10​ns\tau_{\rm{cascade}}\sim 0.1\text{--}10\,\,{\rm ns},[8, 9] determined by the quasiparticle-phonon scattering time at E=3​ΔE=3\Delta. τcascade\tau_{\rm{cascade}} is much shorter than the effective loss time from the film of the excess energy contained in the quasistatic distribution by 2​Δ2\Delta-phonon loss. This time is determined by the effective quasiparticle recombination time of the excess τreff\tau_{r}^{\rm{eff}} provided other relatively slow direct quasiparticle loss-mechanisms such as out-diffusion or tunneling can be ignored. For T/Tc∼0.1T/T_{c}\sim 0.1 and for low detected power, τreff∼ms\tau_{r}^{\rm{eff}}\sim\,\,{\rm ms} even in a thin Al film.[7] Since τreff≫τcascade\tau_{r}^{\rm{eff}}\gg\tau_{\rm{cascade}} the low energy quasistatic population determines the detector response. During the energy relaxation pair-breaking by the emitted phonons occurs provided Ω≥2​Δ\Omega\geq 2\Delta (Ω\Omega is the phonon energy) and this increases the quasistatic population near Δ\Delta, although phonon loss is also possible with characteristic time τl\tau_{l}. At low temperature and low phonon energies Ω∼2​Δ\Omega\sim 2\Delta, the pair-breaking time τp​b​(Ω)∼τ0ϕ\tau_{pb}(\Omega)\sim\tau_{0}^{\phi} where τ0ϕ\tau_{0}^{\phi} is the characteristic phonon lifetime.[10] We assume that τl\tau_{l} is independent of Ω\Omega and is determined by the film thickness and the coupling to the substrate.[11] For thin-films τl\tau_{l} is comparable with, or even less than τp​b\tau_{pb}. Phonon-loss means that energy is lost from any finite thickness film before the quasistatic population is established.

Up to this point we have ignored the effect of the electron-electron interaction in the energy down-conversion. Figure 1 shows the energy dependence of the normal-state scattering rates due to the electron-phonon (e-ϕ\phi) interaction τe​ϕ−1\tau_{e\phi}^{-1},[10] the clean-limit electron-electron (e-e) rate τe​e−1\tau_{ee}^{-1} which is also valid for disordered films at high energies,[8, 12] and the e-e rate including the effect of disorder (τe​e​(D))−1\left(\tau_{ee}\left(D\right)\right)^{-1},[13, 14] where DD denotes the diffusion coefficient. The calculations assume an Al thickness d=35​nmd=35\,\,{\rm nm} with resistivity ρ=8×10−8​Ω​m\rho=8\times 10^{-8}\,\,{\rm\Omega m}, typical of a clean Al film on Al2​O3\rm{Al_{2}O_{3}},[7] that is representative of the thinnest films modeled here. For E>200​ΔE>200\Delta, (τe​ϕ)−1(\tau_{e\phi})^{-1} is cut-off at the Debye energy ΩD\Omega_{D}. At the highest energies E∼104​ΔE\sim 10^{4}\Delta e-e scattering becomes the main energy relaxation mechanism. At lower energies (E∼25​ΔE\sim 25\Delta) disorder increases the e-e rate in this instance. For E∼1.2​ΔE\sim 1.2\Delta we see that the e-e and e-ϕ\phi rates again become equal. For 1.2​Δ<E<104​Δ1.2\Delta<E<10^{4}\Delta the e-ϕ\phi interaction is the principal relaxation mechanism. A detailed description of the energy dependence of the disorder-enhanced e-e rate in a superconductor at low T/TcT/T_{c}, including the effect of the energy gap, seems to be lacking although for E=ΔE=\Delta the e-e rate is further reduced compared to e-ϕ\phi becoming negligible.[15] We note also that the energy scale of interest determining the relative importance of low energy e-e compared to e-ϕ\phi scattering in the relaxation is not Δ\Delta but rather 3​Δ3\Delta: below this energy pair-breaking is forbidden for both. For the thicker Al films discussed below DD is enhanced in clean films so that the effect of disorder is again reduced. For these reasons we ignore e-e relaxation for all energy scales, temperatures and film parameters considered. Extrapolation of our results to other low-TcT_{c} superconductors should thus be done with caution particularly for higher resistivity or very thin films.

A number of calculations exist of ηs\eta_{s} for high energy photons h​νs≫2​Δh\nu_{s}\gg 2\Delta and ΩD\Omega_{D} that have considered infinite superconducting volumes finding ηs∼0.57​– ​0.6\eta_{s}\sim 0.57\text{--\,}0.6 for Al,[8] Nb[16] and Sn.[17] Hijmering et al.[18] calculated quasiparticle creation efficiencies in thin-film Al-Ta bilayers taking account of the modification of the quasiparticle density of states due to the proximity effect but ignored loss of pair-breaking phonons. Zehnder[19] calculated ηs\eta_{s} in a number of thin film superconductors with thickness d=500​nmd=500\,\,{\rm nm} at T=0.5​KT=0.5\,\,{\rm K} including quasiparticle diffusion and phonon loss. ηs\eta_{s} was determined from the number of quasiparticles remaining at time t≃10​nst\simeq 10\,\,{\rm ns} when the initial energy down-conversion was considered complete giving ηs∼0.7\eta_{s}\sim 0.7 for Al.

Here we consider the regime 90≤νs≤450​GHz90\leq\nu_{s}\leq 450\,\,{\rm GHz}. To date no work has calculated ηs\eta_{s} for these signal photon energies at low T/TcT/T_{c}, or the technologically important range of film thicknesses considered here including 2​Δ2\Delta-phonon loss. This frequency range is particularly relevant for mm- and sub-mm astronomy. We have also included a lower frequency probe. We followed Chang and Scalapino[20] to solve the coupled kinetic equations describing the quasiparticle and phonon populations. Our approach explicitly includes the contribution of all phonon branches because it relies on the measured Eliashberg function α2​F​(Ω)\alpha^{2}F(\Omega) in the calculation of the characteristic times[10] and the sum over the three branches is essential to conserve energy.[6]

II The effect of a pair-breaking signal

The coupled kinetic equations described in Ref. 20 were solved using Newton-Raphson iteration to find the non-equilibrium quasiparticle and phonon energy distributions f⁡(E)f(E) and n⁡(Ω)n(\Omega). Details of the scheme are given in Ref. 6. The absorbed powers per unit volume from the signal PsP_{s} and probe PpP_{p} are assumed to be spatially uniform. We ignore changes in Δ\Delta due to PsP_{s} and PpP_{p}. In Ref. 7 we found that changes in Δ\Delta were very small ≪0.001​Δ\ll 0.001\Delta for typical experimental PpP_{p}. The effect of PsP_{s} is to introduce an additional drive term[21] into Eq. [2] of Ref. 6 for the quasiparticle distribution function δ​f​(E)/δ​t|s=Is\delta f(E)/\delta t|_{s}=I_{s} where Is=Bs​KsI_{s}=B_{s}K_{s},

Ks​(E,νs)=Kp​(E,νs)+2​ρ​(E′,Δ)​[1−Δ2E​E′]×[1−f⁡(E)−f⁡(E′)],\begin{split}K_{s}(E,\nu_{s})=K_{p}(E,\nu_{s})&+2\rho(E^{\prime},\Delta)\left[1-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{EE^{\prime}}\right]\\ &\times\left[1-f\left(E\right)-f\left(E^{\prime}\right)\right],\end{split} (1)

E′=h​νs−EE^{\prime}=h\nu_{s}-E and the prefactor BsB_{s} is calculated with Bs=Ps/4N(0)∫Δ∞Eρ(E)Ks(E,νs)dEB_{s}=P_{s}/4N(0)\int_{\Delta}^{\infty}E\rho(E)K_{s}(E,\nu_{s})dE, ensuring that the absorption of PsP_{s} conserves energy. A prefactor for the probe power absorption BpB_{p} can be similarly defined.[6] N⁡(0)N(0) is the single-spin electronic density of states. Some solutions require calculation of differences between distributions. To ensure numerical accuracy we increased the precision requirements in the code so that the errors in the power flow between the quasiparticles and thin-film phonons and then the heat bath phonons (see Ref. 6 for details) were converged to better than 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} and likewise the iterated solutions for BsB_{s} and BpB_{p}. We used a quasiparticle density of states ρ⁡(E,Δ)=Re⁡((E+i​γ)/((E+i​γ)2−Δ2)1/2)\rho(E,\Delta)={\rm Re}\left(\left(E+i\gamma\right)/\left((E+i\gamma\ )^{2}-\Delta^{2}\right)^{1/2}\right). The factor γ\gamma takes account of the broadening of the peak in ρ\rho near E=ΔE=\Delta due to lifetime effects or film inhomogeneity.[1] The choice γ=1.125×10−3​Δ\gamma=1.125\times 10^{-3}\Delta minimizes the difference between the thermal quasiparticle number density NTN_{T} calculated by summing over the discretized distributions (where we used a 1​μ​eV1\,\,{\rm\mu eV} grid) compared to numerical integration of the functions NT=4​N​(0)​∫Δ∞ρ⁡(E,Δ)​f​(E,T)​𝑑EN_{T}=4N(0)\int_{\Delta}^{\infty}\rho(E,\Delta)f(E,T)dE where f⁡(E,T)=1/(1+exp⁡(E/kb​T))f(E,T)=1/\left(1+\exp(E/k_{b}T)\right) is the Fermi-Dirac function and kbk_{b} is Boltzmann’s constant. We used parameters of a thin Al film as in Ref. 6: Δ=180​μ​eV\Delta=180\,\,{\rm\mu eV}, Tc=1.17​KT_{c}=1.17\,\,{\rm K}, N⁡(0)=1.74×104​μ​eV−1​μ​m−3N(0)=1.74\times 10^{4}\,{\rm\mu eV^{-1}\mu m^{-3}}, characteristic quasiparticle time τ0=438​ns\tau_{0}=438\,\,{\rm ns}.[10] τ0ϕ=0.26​ns\tau_{0}^{\phi}=0.26\,\,{\rm ns} and T/Tc=0.1T/T_{c}=0.1. This ratio of τ0/τ0ϕ\tau_{0}/\tau_{0}^{\phi} means that our numerical solutions conserve energy, they are not independent variables: Eq. [11] of Ref. 6 gives the overall parameter dependencies. The value we use for τ0\tau_{0} has given a good account of the temperature dependence of the generation-recombination noise measured in clean, thin Al films.[22, 7] in which the effect of phonon trapping should be small (we estimate τl/τ0ϕ∼0.5\tau_{l}/\tau_{0}^{\phi}\sim 0.5 in this case). A number of previous authors have used τ0∼100​ns\tau_{0}\sim 100\,\,{\rm ns},[23] although this value seems inconsistent with the more recent measurements. Wilson and Prober have also observed unexpectedly long lifetimes in 200​nm200\,\,{\rm nm} Al films (estimating τ0\tau_{0} to be even longer than the value used here), and suggested the observation resulted from an anomalously long τl\tau_{l}.[24] Interestingly the longer τ0\tau_{0} seems to be associated with those measurements that have implemented stringent experimental procedures to minimize the effect of stray light from higher temperature stages in cryogenic systems: note that typical photon energies emitted by a 4​K4\,\,{\rm K} source significantly exceed 2​Δ2\Delta in Al. Where used we assumed h​νp=16​μ​eVh\nu_{p}=16\,\,{\rm\mu eV} (νp=3.88​GHz\nu_{p}=3.88\,\,{\rm GHz}).

III Calculating ηs\eta_{s}

Consider mm, the average number of driven quasistatic quasiparticles generated by each absorbed photon. Signal photons interact with rate ΓΦ=Ps/h​νs\Gamma_{\Phi}=P_{s}/h\nu_{s} and each photon creates two primary quasiparticles. These rapidly relax in energy generating the driven quasistatic population with rate Γs=m​ΓΦ\Gamma_{s}=m\Gamma_{\Phi}. Assuming that all of the excess quasiparticles have E=ΔE=\Delta then ηs=m​Δ/h​νs=Γs​Δ/Ps\eta_{s}=m\Delta/h\nu_{s}=\Gamma_{s}\Delta/P_{s}. We use a modified set of Rothwarf-Taylor rate equations[25] to find Γs\Gamma_{s}. With Γp\Gamma_{p} the generation rate of quasistatic quasiparticles due to the probe, NN the number density of quasiparticles and N2​ΔN_{2\Delta} the number density of 2​Δ2\Delta-phonons

d​Nd​t=Γs+Γp−R​N2+2​β​N2​Δ,\frac{dN}{dt}=\Gamma_{s}+\Gamma_{p}-RN^{2}+2\beta N_{2\Delta}, (2)
d​N2​Δd​t=R​N22−β​N2​Δ−N2​Δ−N2​ΔTτl.\frac{dN_{2\Delta}}{dt}=\frac{RN^{2}}{2}-\beta N_{2\Delta}-\frac{N_{2\Delta}-N_{2\Delta}^{T}}{\tau_{l}}. (3)

Here RR and β\beta are the recombination and pair-breaking coefficients respectively and N2​ΔTN_{2\Delta}^{T} is the thermal density of 2​Δ2\Delta-phonons. We assume that Γs\Gamma_{s} and Γp\Gamma_{p} are independent. With Γs=0\Gamma_{s}=0, Eqs. 2 and 3 can be solved by first also setting Γp=0\Gamma_{p}=0 so that in steady-state, d​N/d​t=d​N2​Δ/d​t=0dN/dt=dN_{2\Delta}/dt=0, giving R​NT2/2=β​N2​ΔTRN_{T}^{2}/2=\beta N_{2\Delta}^{T}. This leads to Γp=R⁡(Np2−NT2)/(β​τl+1)\Gamma_{p}=R\left(N_{p}^{2}-N_{T}^{2}\right)/\left(\beta\tau_{l}+1\right), where NpN_{p} is the total number density of quasiparticles with the probe. For the additional signal Γs\Gamma_{s} we find

Γs=R⁡(N2−Np2)​1β​τl+1.\Gamma_{s}=R\left(N^{2}-N_{p}^{2}\right)\frac{1}{\beta\tau_{l}+1}. (4)

and with β=1/τp​b\beta=1/\tau_{pb}

ηs=R​Δ​(N2−Np2)Ps​1τl/τp​b+1.\eta_{s}=\frac{R\Delta\left(N^{2}-N_{p}^{2}\right)}{P_{s}}\frac{1}{\tau_{l}/\tau_{pb}+1}. (5)

NN and NpN_{p} were calculated by numerically integrating solutions of the coupled kinetic equations. We used Eq. (A9) of Chang and Scalapino[26] to define a recombination rate RCSR_{\rm CS}. We find that setting R≡2​RCSR\equiv 2R_{\rm CS} ensures that the population-averaged recombination time ⟨τr⟩q​p=1/R​N\langle\tau_{r}\rangle_{qp}=1/RN in thermal equilibrium (N=NTN=N_{T}) is the same calculated using either Refs. 26 or 10. We calculate ⟨τp​b⟩ϕ\langle\tau_{pb}\rangle_{\phi} for f⁡(E)f(E) and n⁡(Ω)n(\Omega) using Eq. (A10) of Ref. 26. Writing Eq. 4 in terms of the excess number densities Nse​xN_{s}^{ex} due to the signal and Npe​xN_{p}^{ex} due to the probe alone so that N=Nse​x+Npe​x+NTN=N_{s}^{ex}+N_{p}^{ex}+N_{T} and Np=Npe​x+NTN_{p}=N_{p}^{ex}+N_{T} the effective recombination time τreff=Nse​x/Γs\tau_{r}^{\rm{eff}}=N_{s}^{ex}/\Gamma_{s} can be calculated for any combination of the magnitudes of Nse​xN_{s}^{ex}, Npe​xN_{p}^{ex} and NTN_{T}. In the calculations reported we consider signal and probe powers relevant to ultra-sensitive KIDs for astronomical applications[7] so that N,Np≫NTN,\,\,N_{p}\gg N_{T} for all cases of PpP_{p}, PsP_{s} studied.

IV Results

Fig. 2 shows f⁡(E)f(E) for Pp=20​aW/μ​m3P_{p}=20\,\,{\rm aW/\mu m^{3}}, as the solid curve and the additional effect of Ps/Pp=0.01P_{s}/P_{p}=0.01 (dashed blue curve) with h​νs=5.1​Δh\nu_{s}=5.1\Delta. The inset shows the contribution to the number drive Ks​ρ​(E,Δ)K_{s}\rho(E,\Delta) for the signal normalized so that each absorbed photon produces two quasiparticles per unit time. The double peak arises because Ks​ρ​(E,Δ)K_{s}\rho(E,\Delta) involves the product of final state densities ρ⁡(E,Δ)​ρ​(E′,Δ)\rho(E,\Delta)\rho(E^{\prime},\Delta) which is symmetric with respect to the final state energies. The main figure shows that f⁡(E)f(E) for the probe alone has multiply peaked structure at E∼ΔE\sim\Delta due to absorption of the probe photons by the large density of quasiparticles near Δ\Delta. At energy E=3​ΔE=3\Delta there is a step in f⁡(E)f(E) corresponding to reabsorption of 2​Δ2\Delta-phonons by the driven quasiparticles that also exhibits peaks associated with multiple photon absorption from the probe. A smaller feature at E=3​Δ−h​νpE=3\Delta-h\nu_{p} is visible that arises from stimulated emission.

The dashed curve showing f⁡(E)f(E) with PsP_{s} has similar structure at low energies but now shows a step at E=h​νs−ΔE=h\nu_{s}-\Delta. The curvature f⁡(E)f(E) below this primary peak arises from the energy dependence of the quasiparticle scattering and recombination rates. The peak also has a smaller “satellite” at E=h​νs−Δ+h​νpE=h\nu_{s}-\Delta+h\nu_{p} as multiple photon processes involving signal and probe occur. A further similar feature is evident at E=h​νs+ΔE=h\nu_{s}+\Delta.

Fig. 3 shows the change in contributions to the power flow to the heat bath δ​P​(Ω)ϕ−b=P​(Ω)ϕ−bs−P​(Ω)ϕ−bp\delta P(\Omega)_{\phi-b}=P(\Omega)^{s}_{\phi-b}-P(\Omega)^{p}_{\phi-b}, where P​(Ω)ϕ−bsP(\Omega)^{s}_{\phi-b} is the contribution to the phonon-bath power flow with signal and probe, and P​(Ω)ϕ−bpP(\Omega)^{p}_{\phi-b} that for the probe alone. At low phonon energies Ω<0.3​Δ\Omega<0.3\Delta, δ​P​(Ω)ϕ−b\delta P(\Omega)_{\phi-b} is increased due to pair-breaking. At energies 0.3<Ω<0.5​Δ0.3<\Omega<0.5\Delta the net flow is negative. The first effect arises as the signal itself has a sharply peaked structure near the gap. The reduction arises from the blocking of final states for the scattering of higher energy probe-generated quasiparticles towards the gap. At higher phonon energies there is a significant change in δ​P​(Ω)ϕ−b\delta P(\Omega)_{\phi-b} due to phonons Ω≥2​Δ\Omega\geq 2\Delta. The spectrum also shows a broad low background contribution at all phonon energies Ω≤(h​νs−2​Δ)\Omega\leq\left(h\nu_{s}-2\Delta\right) generated as the primary spectrum scatters to energies E∼ΔE\sim\Delta and at higher Ω\Omega from the highest energy quasiparticles shown in Fig. 2.

Fig. 4 shows calculations of ηs\eta_{s} as a function of h​νsh\nu_{s} for 5 values of τl/τ0ϕ\tau_{l}/\tau_{0}^{\phi}. The calculation used Ps=0.2​aW/μ​m3P_{s}=0.2\,{\rm aW/\mu m^{3}} and Pp=20​aW/μ​m3P_{p}=20\,{\rm aW/\mu m^{3}}. For 2​Δ≤h​νs≤4​Δ2\Delta\leq h\nu_{s}\leq 4\Delta, ηs\eta_{s} reduces monotonically and is independent of the phonon loss time. In this regime the high energy primary quasiparticle peak is created at Δ≤E≤3​Δ\Delta\leq E\leq 3\Delta and phonons emitted in scattering are unable to break pairs. At higher signal energies 4​Δ≤h​νs≤6​Δ4\Delta\leq h\nu_{s}\leq 6\Delta the efficiency tends to increase again and the increase depends on τl/τ0ϕ\tau_{l}/\tau_{0}^{\phi}. Pair-breaking enhances ηs\eta_{s} and the enhancement depends on the probability of pair-breaking compared to other phonon losses. At higher energies multiple pair-breaking is necessary to create the low energy steady state distribution, but multiple phonon loss also occurs. The overall effect is a reduction in ηs\eta_{s} as h​νsh\nu_{s} increases for finite τl/τ0ϕ\tau_{l}/\tau_{0}^{\phi}. We note that ηs→1\eta_{s}\to 1 as h​νs→2​Δh\nu_{s}\to 2\Delta for all τl/τ0ϕ\tau_{l}/\tau_{0}^{\phi} so that Eqs. (2) to (5) and our definition of RR self-consistently conserve energy.

Fig. 5 shows ηs\eta_{s} for h​νs=3​and​  5​Δh\nu_{s}=3{\rm\,and\,\,}5\Delta as a function of PsP_{s} for two values of the probe power. For Pp=0P_{p}=0 the generation efficiency is constant over 5 orders of magnitude of absorbed signal powers. For Pp=20​aW/μ​m3P_{p}=20\,\,{\rm aW/\mu m^{3}} and for low signal power, ηs\eta_{s} is slightly enhanced. We discuss this in the Sec. V.

Fig. 6 shows the distribution-averaged values of τr\tau_{r} associated with the the calculations shown in Fig. 5 (note that Eq. 5 does not involve τr\tau_{r} explicitly) while Fig. 7 shows τp​b\tau_{pb} that is directly used in these calculations. Considering Fig. 6 for the small signal regime Ps≪PpP_{s}\ll P_{p}, NpN_{p} determines τr\tau_{r}. For the large signal regime Ps≫PpP_{s}\gg P_{p}, τr\tau_{r} is independent of PpP_{p} because Nse​xN_{s}^{ex} determines τr\tau_{r}. We see that for fixed h​νsh\nu_{s}, τr\tau_{r} changes by nearly three orders of magnitude whilst ηs\eta_{s} shown in Fig. 5 is constant for all PsP_{s}. (Very close inspection of the results for Pp=0P_{p}=0 would show that ηs\eta_{s} varies for the range of calculated PsP_{s} by about ±0.03%\pm 0.03\% which we consider acceptable given the numerical precision used and the discretization of the distributions.) Also τr\tau_{r} for the two signal photon energies differ, but the generation rate of excess quasiparticles depends on h​νsh\nu_{s}, as does the fraction of power lost before the quasistatic driven distributions are created. We would note that Eq. 5 correctly takes into account these underlying changes in τr\tau_{r} due to signal and probe.

Fig. 7 shows that the distribution-averaged τp​b∼τ0ϕ\tau_{pb}\sim\tau_{0}^{\phi}, which would often be assumed, but moreover τp​b<τ0ϕ\tau_{pb}<\tau_{0}^{\phi}. For T/Tc=0.1T/T_{c}=0.1, τp​b​(Ω)≤τp​b​(2​Δ)\tau_{pb}(\Omega)\leq\tau_{pb}(2\Delta). τp​b​(Ω)\tau_{pb}(\Omega) scales approximately as 1/Ω1/\Omega in thermal equilibrium,[10] hence the slight reduction when τp​b\tau_{pb} is calculated for the non-equlibrium distributions. We find that the variation of τp​b\tau_{pb} as a function of the drive (both probe and signal) arises from the detailed spectra of the 2​Δ2\Delta-phonons for each case and is (to first-order) independent of the quasiparticle spectrum. It is possible to define an effective phonon temperature T2​ΔeffT_{2\Delta}^{\rm{eff}} that accounts for the total number of 2​Δ2\Delta-phonons. This approach accounts for the calculated τp​b\tau_{pb} to within 1%~1\%, but not for the detailed behavior as a function of PsP_{s}. In the presence of the probe and signal the probe determines τp​b\tau_{pb} if Pp≫PsP_{p}\gg P_{s} and in this case we find T2​ΔeffT_{2\Delta}^{\rm{eff}} more closely accounts for the calculated τp​b\tau_{pb}. We would emphasize here that the full calculation of τp​b\tau_{pb} is necessary to find that ηs\eta_{s} is independent of power PsP_{s}.

V Discussion and Conclusions

We have presented calculations of the quasiparticle generation efficiency ηs\eta_{s} for a pair-breaking signal in thin Al films at T/Tc=0.1T/T_{c}=0.1 with photon energies in the range 2​Δ≤h​νs≤10​Δ2\Delta\leq h\nu_{s}\leq 10\Delta, 90≤νs≤450​GHz90\leq\nu_{s}\leq 450\,\,{\rm GHz}. We have also investigated the effect of including a probe with power and frequency typical of those used in low-noise KID readout. The calculated detailed spectra show the effects of multiple interactions of the probe and the signal in the driven f⁡(E)f(E) with structure for example at E=h⁡(νs+νp)E=h(\nu_{s}+\nu_{p}). Our results demonstrate the importance of phonon loss on the quasiparticle creation efficiency. For thick films, τl/τ0ϕ=8\tau_{l}/\tau_{0}^{\phi}=8, our calculations are in general agreement with earlier work for much higher signal energies, in calculations that ignore 2​Δ2\Delta-phonon loss, showing ηs≃0.59\eta_{s}~\simeq 0.59. For resonators, thinner films would tend to be used since these maximize the kinetic inductance fraction of the response,[1] but these have reduced creation efficiencies by as much as 40%40\% for the thinnest films considered here. Our calculations establish limits on the detection sensitivity of thin-film superconductors. The limiting Noise Equivalent Power of a thin-film detector is determined by generation-recombination noise[24, 27, 6] and is given by N​E​P=2​Δ​N​V/τreff/ηNEP=2\Delta\sqrt{NV/\tau_{r}^{\rm{eff}}}/\eta where VV is the volume of the film and η\eta the overall detection efficiency. η\eta is the product of all detection efficiencies (including coupling efficiency) but ηs\eta_{s} shown in Fig. 4 determines the limiting efficiency in the thin-film case. Fig. [8] of Ref. 6 shows calculations of the limiting coupled ​N​E​P{\emph{NEP}} for η=0.59\eta=0.59 and 11 as a function of absorbed probe power. The present work shows that the best-possible coupled ​N​E​P​s{\emph{NEPs}} are even higher than the case η=0.59\eta=0.59 shown there for much of the mm- and sub-mm spectrum in thin superconducting films. In deriving Eq. 5 we assumed that all quasiparticles have energy Δ\Delta. It is possible to take account of the energy distribution of the excess quasiparticles in the derivation and this would increase our calculated ηs\eta_{s} by about 4%4\%, but for consistency with earlier work we have assumed E=ΔE=\Delta for all of the excess.

We identify a coupling between the signal and probe that enhances ηs\eta_{s} by about 2%2\%. This maybe the effect described by Gulian and van Vechten,[28] who suggested that for low PsP_{s} multiple probe photon absorption by the higher energy primary peak of Fig. 2 (inset) occurs and some fraction of these quasiparticles are driven to energies E≥3​ΔE\geq 3\Delta. By contrast Fig. 2 suggests that 2​Δ2\Delta-phonon reabsorption occurs to enhance ηs\eta_{s}. As the signal power increases there is a slight reduction in ηs\eta_{s} because the relevant quantity is the fraction of quasiparticles in the photon peak driven above the pair-breaking threshold. The fraction reduces because the probe power is fixed and the probe generates (most of) the excess 2​Δ2\Delta-phonons. In future work we intend to extend the work to consider other low temperature superconductors, to investigate the detection linearity of a resonator with the driven distributions and also to consider the probe power levels that optimize detector N​E​P​sNEPs.
